questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.3 & 0.8 \\ 0.7 & 0.2\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}0.1 \\ 0.9\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $q$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $q$ is a stochastic vector

II. $Pq=q$

III. $q$ is a steady-state vector of $P$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that $Pq=q.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

- Statement II is false. Note that

$$
Pq=[\begin{aligned}0.3 & 0.8 \\ 0.7 & 0.2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.1 \\ 0.9\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.03+0.72 \\ 0.07+0.18\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.75 \\ 0.25\end{aligned}]\ne q.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $Pq\ne q,$ it is not a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & 0.9\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & 0.9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.1 \\ 0.6 & -0.1\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{7}{6}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{6}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{7} \\ \frac{6}{7}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{1}{7}-\frac{6}{7}=-\frac{5}{7}.$

questions.problem:
There are two groups of people In a small town: those who travel to work by car and those who travel by train. Every year a study is done in which people are asked about their preference between using trains versus cars. The table below shows the results of this study.
From:
Car Train
To: Car $0.35$ $0.25$
Train $0.65$ $0.75$
It's found that $65%$ of people who currently travel by car will switch to train next year, while $25%$ of people who currently travel by train will switch to their car next year. Assuming that the town has $90\,000$ people that travel to work by train or car, and the given probabilities remain constant over many years, how many people will eventually use the train to travel to work?
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.35 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & 0.75\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 \\ 0.65 & -0.25\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0.65 & -0.25 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.65 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{18}{13}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{13}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{18} \\ \frac{13}{18}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, $\frac{13}{18}$ of the people will eventually use the train to travel. Therefore, the number of people who will eventually use the train is

$$
\frac{13}{18}\cdot 90\,000=65\,000.
$$

The migration table below describes the movement of the population between cities and suburbs every year in a certain state.
From:
Cities Suburbs
To: Cities $0.8$ $0.7$
Suburbs $0.2$ $0.3$
That is, $20%$ of those living in cities move to the suburbs each year, and $70%$ of those living in suburbs move to the cities. Assuming that the population of the state is $9$ million and remains constant, how many people would eventually live in cities if the given probabilities remain constant over many years?
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & 0.3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & 0.3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & -0.7\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -0.7 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{9}{2}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{2}{9}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{7}{9}$ of the $9$ million population will live in cities. Therefore, the total number of people living in cities after many years will be

$$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 5 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 19 & -19 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{3}-8{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}={x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 3{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.4 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 2 & 0 \\ -6 & 4 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -10 & 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & -14 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -10 & 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{14}{10}{x}_{3}=\frac{7}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}+2(\frac{7}{5}{x}_{3})-6{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{8}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{7}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{5}{x}_{3}+\frac{7}{5}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{20}{5}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{7}{20} \\ \frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{2}{5}+\frac{7}{20}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{10}{20}=\frac{1}{2}.

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.25\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & -0.8 & 0.65 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & -0.75\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.2 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.3 & -0.8 & 0.65 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 & -0.75 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 3 & -8 & 6.5 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & -7.5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-3{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}+0.5{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{2}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
A study shows how the sports preferences of young people in a certain community vary from year to year. The following table shows the results of this study.
From:
Baseball Basketball Football
To: Baseball $0.8$ $0.2$ $0$
Basketball $0.1$ $0.6$ $0.2$
Football $0.1$ $0.2$ $0.8$
For example, $10%$ of people who used to prefer baseball now prefer football. Given that $1\,260$ young people were interviewed for the study and that the probabilities listed remain constant for many years, how many of those people will eventually prefer baseball?
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.8\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.2\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & -0.2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -4 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+0{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{7}{3}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{3}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{7} \\ \frac{2}{7} \\ \frac{3}{7}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{2}{7}$ of the people will prefer baseball. Therefore, the number of people who will prefer baseball is

$$
\frac{2}{7}\cdot 1\,260=360\,\text{people}.
$$

questions.problem:
A study conducted on $3\,400$ teenagers by the transportation department of a particular city reveals that teenagers' preference for the type of home-to-school transportation changes with time. The following table shows the results of this study.
From:
Bus Bicycle Electric Scooter
To: Bus $0.2$ $0.2$ $0$
Bicycle $0.4$ $0.4$ $0.4$
Electric Scooter $0.4$ $0.4$ $0.6$
For example, $40%$ of teenagers who used to go to school by bus now go by bicycle. How many teenagers would eventually go to school on electric scooters if the listed probabilities remained constant over many years?
questions.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. 
As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.2 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.8 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.8 & 0.2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & -0.4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=5{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=5{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{5}{2}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+(\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3})-{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{4}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}+\frac{4}{5}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 2{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{4}{10} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{1}{2}$ of the teenagers will go to school in electric scooters. Therefore, the total number of teenagers in the city that will go to school in electric scooters will be

$$
\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\,400=1\,700.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Steady-State Vectors of Stochastic Matrices

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 2x2 Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
The table below describes how the customers of a particular electronics store feel about their next computer purchase.
From:
Laptop Desktop
To: Laptop $0.9$ $0.8$
Desktop $0.1$ $0.2$
It is found that $10 \%$ of customers who currently use a laptop would choose a desktop on their next purchase, while $80 \%$ of customers who currently use a desktop would choose a laptop on their next purchase. Given that the store has $5\,400$ customers, all of whom purchase a new computer every two years, how many customers would eventually own a desktop computer if the given probabilities remain constant over many two-year periods?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/30bdf02b3878802e65a722f40ba1f02a1e27be8004a6bc19a31073c9a46fdd1a.svg)

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many two-year periods, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/7d76dd51e6a18be167b9f8d477475f0b2c50c799f763b59b77f7b94a54b45d22.svg)

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.8 & 0 \\ 0.1 & -0.8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.1 & 0.8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=8{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/96ec226492c36f9e4ea589ac736b296548489a6d076cfaf85f672eccf12b4992.svg)

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ 9{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Our steady-state vector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/47dc46374390a39e38c4888c470b6c8f545b500a4fe07b8f0c92a07c9783df9a.svg)

So, ${\color{blue}{\dfrac{1}{9}}}$ of the $5\,400$ customers would eventually own a desktop computer. Therefore, the total number of people who would eventually own a desktop computer is

$$
\dfrac{1}{9} \cdot 5\,400 = 600.
$$

Example: 
                    Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/4144387d792ca55ab5bece21ba7feffcf777ab88d922e116f06f561e300ddd03.svg)

Find the steady-state vector $\mathbf q$ of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/b25aca881e2fbbdbcc00440f2b2b0e99876a860d78182b4dc0c2f860fc92cb8f.svg)

The matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.9 & 0.3 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -0.7 & 0.1 & 0 \\ 0.7 & 0.4 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=20{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=20{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-18 & 6 & 10 & 0 \\ 2 & -7 & 1 & 0 \\ 14 & 8 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 & 1 & 0 \\ -18 & 6 & 10 & 0 \\ 14 & 8 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+9{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-7{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -57 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 57 & -19 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -57 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
x_2=\dfrac{1}{3}x_3.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2x_1 -7\left(\dfrac{1}{3}x_3\right) + x_3 = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x_1 = \dfrac{2}{3}x_3.
$$

Hence, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/3a15042dcfc8fd35e5c8052bb3beb819f1d35b43b18d84860e28461ec6f3d07f.svg)

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{3}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 2{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, our steady-state vector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/372d38d88399113400ab1e52a1f23ce2db1fcc3a9c6a05a9073808ea89a4043e.svg)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic 3x3 Matrix

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

- $6\%$ of the city population relocates to the countryside,

- $3\%$ of the countryside population relocates to the city, and

- everyone else remains where they are.

Additionally, $70\%$ of the population lived in the city and $30\%$ in the countryside at the time of the study. 

We can represent this situation using a stochastic matrix $P$ and initial state vector $\mathbf x_0,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/44fa9ad32622bd1d7b3541206030ecc862a3db9420f46049c9f16992fdb947ca.svg) 

As we've seen, to find the state vector $\mathbf x_{k+1}$ that corresponds to the $(k+1)$th year, we left-multiply the state vector corresponding to the $k$th year by $P.$ This gives rise to the following Markov chain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

The local authority wants to determine whether the state vectors settle down to a fixed state. With the aid of a computer, they compute the following states:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0.636\,97 \\ 0.363\,03\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0.609\,64 \\ 0.390\,36\end{aligned}] \\  & ⋮ \\ {x}_{100} & =P{x}_{99}=[\begin{aligned}0.333\,363 \\ 0.666\,637\end{aligned}]≈[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{101} & =P{x}_{100}=[\begin{aligned}0.333\,36 \\ 0.666\,64\end{aligned}]≈[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the data, we see that the vectors $\mathbf x_{100}$ and $\mathbf x_{101}$ are both approximately equal to the vector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/030d5719a268d9e15c2c58488ff1c36602d5c757475e79c25dcd1da5a4eb8712.svg)

Furthermore, computing $\mathbf x_{102}, \mathbf{x}_{103}, \ldots$ all give vectors approximately equal to $\mathbf q.$ This suggests that the sequence $\mathbf x_k$ converges to $\mathbf q\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_k \rightarrow \mathbf q \quad\textrm{as}\quad k\to\infty.
$$

The vector $\mathbf q$ is called a **steady-state vector** of the matrix $P.$ Here, our steady-state vector suggests that after enough time has passed, one-third of the population will live in the city and two-thirds will live in the countryside.

Finally, notice that for large values of $k,$ we have

$$
P\mathbf x_k \approx \mathbf x_{k}.
$$

This observation indicates how to find $\mathbf q$ without resorting to computers.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

- $6\%$ of the city population relocates to the countryside,

- $3\%$ of the countryside population relocates to the city, and

- everyone else remains where they are.

Additionally, $70\%$ of the population lived in the city and $30\%$ in the countryside at the time of the study. 

We can represent this situation using a stochastic matrix $P$ and initial state vector $\mathbf x_0,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/44fa9ad32622bd1d7b3541206030ecc862a3db9420f46049c9f16992fdb947ca.svg) 

As we've seen, to find the state vector $\mathbf x_{k+1}$ that corresponds to the $(k+1)$th year, we left-multiply the state vector corresponding to the $k$th year by $P.$ This gives rise to the following Markov chain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

The local authority wants to determine whether the state vectors settle down to a fixed state. With the aid of a computer, they compute the following states:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0.636\,97 \\ 0.363\,03\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0.609\,64 \\ 0.390\,36\end{aligned}] \\  & ⋮ \\ {x}_{100} & =P{x}_{99}=[\begin{aligned}0.333\,363 \\ 0.666\,637\end{aligned}]≈[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{101} & =P{x}_{100}=[\begin{aligned}0.333\,36 \\ 0.666\,64\end{aligned}]≈[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the data, we see that the vectors $\mathbf x_{100}$ and $\mathbf x_{101}$ are both approximately equal to the vector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/030d5719a268d9e15c2c58488ff1c36602d5c757475e79c25dcd1da5a4eb8712.svg)

Furthermore, computing $\mathbf x_{102}, \mathbf{x}_{103}, \ldots$ all give vectors approximately equal to $\mathbf q.$ This suggests that the sequence $\mathbf x_k$ converges to $\mathbf q\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_k \rightarrow \mathbf q \quad\textrm{as}\quad k\to\infty.
$$

The vector $\mathbf q$ is called a **steady-state vector** of the matrix $P.$ Here, our steady-state vector suggests that after enough time has passed, one-third of the population will live in the city and two-thirds will live in the countryside.

Finally, notice that for large values of $k,$ we have

$$
P\mathbf x_k \approx \mathbf x_{k}.
$$

This observation indicates how to find $\mathbf q$ without resorting to computers.

tutorials.name: Steady-State Vectors
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have a stochastic matrix $P$ and a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}.$ Then, $\mathbf{q}$ is a **steady-state vector** of $P$ if 

$$
P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.
$$

For example, to show that the stochastic vector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/caba3c1b2f3245a3ebea0bd6ff6d47c63d409a7ba18a48db1f1269cb9ac13854.svg) 

is a steady-state vector for the stochastic matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/7f231d09e7daf85eec90e682a9eb53c242aadac75b372e3685b65757ae3309dc.svg) 

we compute the matrix product $P\mathbf q\mathbin:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =[\begin{aligned}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0.94+2\cdot 0.03 \\ 0.06+2\cdot 0.97\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =q\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since $P\mathbf q = \mathbf q,$ the vector $\mathbf q$ is a steady-state vector of $P.$

$$

For example, to show that the stochastic vector

we compute the matrix product $P\mathbf q\mathbin:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =[\begin{aligned}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0.94+2\cdot 0.03 \\ 0.06+2\cdot 0.97\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =q\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since $P\mathbf q = \mathbf q,$ the vector $\mathbf q$ is a steady-state vector of $P.$

tutorials.name: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic Matrix
tutorials.problem:
To find a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P,$ we seek a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that 

$$
P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.
$$

Let's begin by writing this equation in a slightly different form:

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector we seek is a solution to the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's use this idea to find a steady-state vector for the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/77ffe4078d3c62c30ab94b59bc9465a92db659b9e70b137bb144deb44844e800.svg)

First, we compute $(P-I):$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/3d91ece6103baa469569adf1994f3965cfc3429fbe65c0d7cfffff53b83b20ef.svg)

Then, to solve $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0},$ we reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
x_1= \dfrac 23 x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/4a5d81320f3e4eeee6b9fb09424238467d6c9e8b2e2246971ba3550b65a6d9c2.svg)

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{3}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, our steady-state vector is

tutorials.title: Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic Matrix
tutorials.content:
To find a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P,$ we seek a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that 

$$
P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.
$$

Let's begin by writing this equation in a slightly different form:

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector we seek is a solution to the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's use this idea to find a steady-state vector for the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/77ffe4078d3c62c30ab94b59bc9465a92db659b9e70b137bb144deb44844e800.svg)

First, we compute $(P-I):$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/3d91ece6103baa469569adf1994f3965cfc3429fbe65c0d7cfffff53b83b20ef.svg)

Then, to solve $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0},$ we reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
x_1= \dfrac 23 x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/4a5d81320f3e4eeee6b9fb09424238467d6c9e8b2e2246971ba3550b65a6d9c2.svg)

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{3}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, our steady-state vector is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/8515cb27fa64a5186fae0c63184df2ff7651c03963eef5804c4d6bedbace2283.svg)

tutorials.name: Regular Stochastic Matrices
tutorials.problem:
A stochastic matrix $P$ is **regular** if there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $P^n$ has all positive elements.

Let's consider some examples:

- The stochastic matrix $P,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/e9588bb9c77762d6caee5460403077eba65a891676f85a9e30ff99e7e6112184.svg) 
has all positive elements. Therefore, it is a regular stochastic matrix.

- The stochastic matrix $Q,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/e0ba33618820d19e77d365a9f316239ef2e36133cbcac4007bf2b5c2f6e57137.svg) 
contains a zero element. However, if we compute its square, we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/29c5a411ac3c797699a39e35972e415e98df3347e66581bb5494f61a92d92bd5.svg) 
which has all positive elements. Therefore, $Q$ is a regular stochastic matrix.

Regular stochastic matrices have the following important property:

*Any regular stochastic matrix has a **unique** steady-state vector $\mathbf q.$ Moreover, the Markov chain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

converges to $\mathbf q$ for **any** initial state $\mathbf x_0.$*

tutorials.title: Regular Stochastic Matrices
tutorials.content:
A stochastic matrix $P$ is **regular** if there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $P^n$ has all positive elements.

Let's consider some examples:

- The stochastic matrix $P,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/e9588bb9c77762d6caee5460403077eba65a891676f85a9e30ff99e7e6112184.svg) 
has all positive elements. Therefore, it is a regular stochastic matrix.

- The stochastic matrix $Q,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14235560/assets/e0ba33618820d19e77d365a9f316239ef2e36133cbcac4007bf2b5c2f6e57137.svg) 
contains a zero element. However, if we compute its square, we get
